If I could change one thing about iOS 27 and iPadOS 27, it would be disabling the new swipe-down gesture for invoking Siri AI. There are already plenty of ways to summon Siri without breaking the muscle memory I've built for opening Notification Center on my iPhone and iPad.

Meanwhile, on the Mac side, macOS 27 Golden Gate is almost entirely good news. Even as late as the end of August, new betas are still adding welcome changes. Still, before macOS 27 ships next month, there is one adjustment I would like to see.

MacBook battery percentage is harder to read in macOS 27 Golden Gate

macOS 27 Golden Gate includes a redesigned battery control for the menu bar. By default, the percentage is not shown — only a battery-shaped visual indicator icon.

In that state, it looks fine. I also turn off the percentage display on my iPhone, which has the same battery icon. However, I've always preferred showing the percentage on my Mac.

If you turn on the "Show Percentage" option in macOS 27 Golden Gate, it puts the number inside the battery icon. I assume this is meant to align with the design choice Apple made on iPhone with iOS 27.

Putting the percentage inside the battery icon on iPhone was Apple's way of addressing the spatial density issue of fitting everything to the right of the notch or Dynamic Island. On the Mac, however — even in the menu bar — I don't have that screen space problem.

I've been running macOS 27 Golden Gate on my 15-inch MacBook Air since the first developer beta dropped on day one. I've noticed I'm generally paying less attention to the battery percentage, because it's harder on my eyes to make out.

I hope Apple reconsiders this design decision down the road, especially if more users run into the same issue. Until then, I've at least solved the problem for myself.

I built a simple menu bar utility with Codex that clearly presents the current battery status and percentage, with the visual clarity I expected. If you think this tool might help you too, you can download and install it for free here.
